extracted.intended_audience: students, historians, and readers interested in the history of advertising and promotional practices
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-length historical account of 18th-century advertising practices (quack medicines, Graham's Temple/Celestial Bed, state and private lotteries), illustrating techniques used to attract, persuade, and monetize audiences. Useful as examples/case-studies of promotional tactics and messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle and sensory showmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of lavish visual and sensory effects to attract crowds: 'magnificent illuminations', 'enchanted palace', 'mirrors', 'electrical apparatus', 'Oriental odours', 'musical' accompaniments, and 'Elysian promenades'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine lighting, music, scent, luxurious décor and exotic props to create an overwhelming sensory environment that draws attendance and conveys uniqueness ('the Temple ... sweetly illuminated', 'Oriental odours and setherial essences will perfume the air'). Hire striking actors/figures (e.g., 'two sons of Anak') to increase visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bombastic, extravagant copy and grandiose claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of flamboyant, hyperbolic language and grand claims in adverts and handbills: the Doctor's 'general bombastic style' and copy declaring the place 'more riches... than any royal Palace in the world'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ over-the-top rhetoric and superlatives to excite curiosity and convey superiority; long, emphatic adverts and handbills are used to impress and lure ('the magnificent Electrical Apparatus... the supremely brilliant and unique decorations').

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantified testimonials and named case-lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing numbers and particulars of cures with patient names and residences: 'particulars of several hundred Cures ... with the Names and Residence of the Patients'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List counts of successes and include identifying details to suggest transparency and verifiable results; offer small-priced pamphlets containing these particulars as social proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization via exclusive, high-priced services
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering expensive, exclusive experiences for direct payment (e.g., the Celestial Bed charged 'one hundred pounds per night', later reduced to 'twenty-five pounds').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create premium-priced, limited-access offerings (tickets, nights, private admissions, bank-bill deposits) to monetize curiosity and signal exclusivity; adjust pricing when demand falls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancillary product sales alongside exhibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Selling pamphlets, private advisers, treatises, and medicines at the Temple: 'A Pamphlet is now published... price only 3d.' and 'All Dr. Graham's Medicines to be had as usual, at the Temple of Health.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage events/exhibitions to retail related printed works and remedies; use exhibitions as distribution points for branded goods and paid literature (varying price points from cheap pamphlets to 'Private Advisers' at a guinea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mythic/religious framing and institutional branding
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing commercial offerings with sacred/mythic titles and institutions: 'Temple of Health', 'Temple of Hymen', 'Holy of Holies', 'Celestial Bed'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt quasi-religious or mythic naming and ritualized presentation to confer novelty, authority, and emotional resonance upon an offering ('Introductory Oration... the whole Art of enjoying Health').

rubrics_metrics.name: Assurances of decency to broaden audience (esp. women)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit promises to avoid offence and maintain decorum to reassure female and genteel patrons: 'Ladies of rank and character are assured, that nothing will be said or seen, which can give even the smallest offence... and that every thing will be conducted with the most perfect decency and decorum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear statements of propriety in promotions to reduce barriers for women and respectable audiences, encouraging attendance and purchase by signalling safe, genteel entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staged demonstrations and recurring programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly scheduled exhibitions, lectures and live demonstrations as the core offering: 'the Exhibitions at the Temple of Health will be continued ... every Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday Evenings' and lectures 'will be repeated This and every Evening this Week'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program recurring events and demonstrations (lectures, displays of apparatus) to build habit and enable repeat attendance; advertise schedules and ticket prices prominently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Street promotion and direct distribution (handbills/agents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of street agents and handbills to disseminate adverts: 'he hired two men of extraordinary stature... to distribute bills from house to house' and 'These handbills were curiously suggestive of the wonderful Doctor's general bombastic style.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ on-the-ground promoters and printed handbills to reach broad audiences; use striking costumes/characters to amplify distribution impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of named addresses, opening times, and admission pricing
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing practical details in adverts to facilitate attendance: addresses ('Pall Mall, nearly opposite the King's Palace'), viewing times ('from two o'Clock in the Afternoon till eight at Night'), and admission ('Admittance 5s.', 'Admittance only One Shilling').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear logistical information — location, hours, admission fees — so interested people can attend; vary tiers of access (cheap viewing vs. paid body of the hall) to segment audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to exotic/pseudoscientific authority (electricity, magnetism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking contemporary science or exotic arts to lend credibility and novelty: promises to explain 'the true Nature and Effects of Electricity, Air, Music, and Magnetism' and reference to 'magnetico-electric' bed and 'celestial fire'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associate offerings with fashionable scientific or exotic concepts to appear modern/authoritative and to intrigue customers; pair spectacle with pseudo-technical explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lottery advertising: publicizing prior wins to build credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Lottery-offices 'sedulous to tell how many of the grand prizes had in former years fallen to the lot of persons who had bought at his shop.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertise past winners linked to a seller/office to create a perception of luck and credibility that drives future purchases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lottery fractional shares to broaden affordability and market
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractors divided shares 'into halves, quarters, eighths, and sixteenths' so 'a man with thirty shillings to spare could buy a sixteenth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer fractional participation in high-value tickets to allow lower-income buyers to engage, expanding the customer base and increasing aggregate sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of woodcuts, verses and simple visuals to attract uneducated buyers
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional materials employed 'Woodcuts and copies of verses ... suited to attract the uneducated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include bold visuals and simple, catchy verse in printed adverts to reach less-literate audiences and increase impulse purchases.

rubrics_metrics.name: State or official framing as a trust signal in lotteries
rubrics_metrics.description: State-run framing and contractor arrangements: 'The State lottery was framed on the simple principle... The Government gave £10 in prizes for every share taken on an average', and contractors took shares/contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use governmental or official associations (or the appearance thereof) to signal legitimacy and encourage participation in large-scale gambling/promo schemes.
